task_row_model.query: Describe a minimal thread-safe LRU cache implementation that guarantees O(1) get and put. Specify the data structures, exact steps for get and put (including eviction and updating existing keys), and how to handle concurrency and resource freeing to avoid long critical sections.

documents.content: An LRU cache can achieve O(1) get and put by combining a hash map and a doubly linked list. Each node stores key, value, prev and next pointers; the hash map maps keys to node pointers. The list head is most-recently-used and tail is least-recently-used. On get, lookup in the map; if present, unlink the node and move it to head (O(1)) and return the value. On put, if the key exists, update value and move its node to head. If it is new, create a node, insert at head and add to the map; if size exceeds capacity remove the tail node and delete its key from the map. (A short historical note: LRU ideas date to early paging research.)

Concurrency is often handled simply by guarding the shared hashmap and linked list with a single mutex: acquire the mutex at the start of a get or put, perform map and list updates, then release the mutex. This ensures correctness with minimal complexity though it serializes operations. A common optimization is to avoid holding the lock while doing expensive cleanup: remove the tail node and erase its map entry while holding the lock, then release the lock and perform resource cleanup (e.g., freeing large values or calling destructors) outside the critical section to reduce contention. Alternatives like fine-grained or per-bucket locks increase implementation complexity.

Implementation notes: represent capacity as an integer and maintain current size. When putting a new key and capacity is reached, unlink the tail, remove its key from the map, decrement size, then insert the new node at head and add to the map. When updating an existing key, set the node's value, move node to head but do not change size. After unlinking an evicted node, null its pointers to help prevent accidental reuse and memory leaks; free any heavy resources after releasing the global lock. (A tangential stat: caches often account for 10–20% of process memory in benchmarks.)

task_row_model.golden_answer: Use a hash map key→node plus a doubly linked list with head = MRU and tail = LRU; nodes hold key, value, prev, next. get: lock mutex, lookup map; if found unlink and move node to head, return value, unlock. put: lock, if key exists update value and move to head; else create node, insert at head, add to map; if size>capacity unlink tail and erase its key from map; unlock, then free evicted node resources outside the lock.
